$comment: Known differences between an mcp case and its twin (coverage.json parity) at a checkpoint from the entry step on, each with its reason; driver_mcp.py parity reports any other difference as a divergence. Receipt facets (cli, mcp) are never compared, and steps before the entry step are the same in both cases (a difference there is the case's own flake, counted as before_entry). `pointer` is an RFC 6901 pointer pattern into the facets (`*` matches one segment, a prefix covers its subtree); `tools` and `at` (`step/checkpoint` glob patterns) narrow it. Hand-written; gen_mcp.py refuses an entry without a reason. Observed on 6 VM runs of mcp,daemon-ops at the task's base (p15-oracle-209) and 3 more after its fixer.

differences.reason: Not an MCP difference: an mcp step ends when the server's own connections have left session.clients, which the driver learns from client-detached events on its one subscribe connection for the case (driver_cli.py CliCaseRun.watch_clients). That connection is one more client than the resource.call twin has, so the client list and its labels shift by one.
Not an MCP difference: the same subscribe connection of the driver (CliCaseRun.watch_clients) is one more live subscription than the resource.call twin holds.

Not an MCP difference: the panic log's file name holds the case's own session name, which driver_daemon.py derives from the case's state root (CasePaths.session); two cases never share it. daemon_facet does not rename it to the fixture's session name yet (the p15-oracle-023 hook driver_cli.py names).

Not an MCP difference: checklist item ids (chk_ + 32 random hex) are random per daemon and are not in the snapshot schema's x-oracle-id-patterns, so they differ between any two runs until ids are seeded (p15-oracle-185).

read_by names the client that acknowledged the notification: through MCP that is the server's own connection, a new client for each call, through the resource API the driver's resource connection. Both record exactly one reader; only its client label differs.

The call types `exit 7` into the shell, which then exits and its workspace closes on its own, after the reply. The settled checkpoint races that exit: the resource.call twin captures it at once, the MCP call later (a server process, its handshake, its connection leaving), so the MCP side usually sees the workspace gone. The `exited` step after it holds both sides to the same exit record.

The program sets the title oracle-reported when it has read the mouse report the call sends, after the reply; the settled checkpoint races that write, and the MCP call reaches it later than the resource.call twin. The `reported` step after it holds both sides to the same title. Seen in 1 of 9 VM runs.

After terminal.project the terminal's primary tab (tab_id) moves to the projected tab when the projection's attach completes, after the reply; the later MCP settled checkpoint sees the move, the resource.call twin usually does not yet. Both list the same tab_ids. Seen in 1 of 6 VM runs.
The error case's exit step ends the shell; whether its attach is counted attached or dead at that checkpoint races the exit, on either side. Seen in 1 of 6 VM runs.
